title: Reproductive Organ Location and Boundaries
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter places the reproductive organs in the pelvis, perineum, and chest wall and explains what holds each one in position. It covers the broad ligament and pelvic peritoneal pouches, the named ligaments of the uterus and ovary and the vessels they carry, pelvic floor support and prolapse, the coverings of the testis and spermatic cord, the position and fibrous framework of the breast, the erectile bodies of the penis, and the boundaries of the perineum with the prostate behind them. Board questions link a structure to its contents, its blood supply, its embryological origin, or the sign that appears when it tears, stretches, or is invaded by tumor. Knowing the layer or ligament involved predicts the finding.
prerequisites: Layers of the anterior abdominal wall and the inguinal canal
Parietal and visceral peritoneum, mesenteries, and intraperitoneal versus retroperitoneal organs
Branches of the abdominal aorta and internal iliac artery
Bony pelvis: pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrum, and coccyx
Descent of the gonads and the gubernaculum (reproductive embryology)

connections.how: The gubernaculum and processus vaginalis explain why the round ligament and the spermatic cord both pass through the inguinal canal.
Indirect inguinal hernias and hydroceles follow a patent processus vaginalis inside the coverings of the cord.
The ureter runs beside the suspensory ligament at the pelvic brim and beneath the uterine artery near the cervix, so pelvic disease and surgery can involve it.
Ectopic pregnancy, endometriosis, breast carcinoma, and prostate carcinoma present through the anatomy of the pouches, ligaments, and zones described here.
Gonadal lymph drains to para-aortic nodes while scrotal and vulvar skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes, which predicts where tumors spread.

terms.def: A double fold of peritoneum that runs from the lateral uterus to the lateral pelvic wall and floor and encloses the uterine tube, ovarian attachments, and uterine vessels.
The peritoneal recess between the uterus and rectum that forms the lowest part of the female peritoneal cavity in the upright position; also called the pouch of Douglas or cul-de-sac.
A peritoneal fold from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall that carries the ovarian vessels, lymphatics, and nerves; also called the infundibulopelvic ligament.
The embryonic fibrous cord that guides gonadal descent; in the female it persists as the ovarian ligament and the round ligament.
The broad muscle sheet of the pelvic floor, formed by puborectalis, pubococcygeus, and iliococcygeus, whose tone supports the pelvic organs.
A fibromuscular mass between the vagina (or bulb of the penis) and the anal canal where several perineal muscles and the external anal sphincter converge.
Descent of the uterus, vaginal apex, bladder, rectum, or small bowel into or through the vaginal canal because its supports have failed.
An outpouching of peritoneum that precedes the testis through the inguinal canal; its distal part becomes the tunica vaginalis.
The network of testicular veins in the spermatic cord that surrounds the testicular artery and cools arterial blood by countercurrent heat exchange.
Fibrous bands (Cooper ligaments) that run from the dermis through the breast to the deep fascia and support the breast tissue.
The dense collagenous sheath around each erectile body, thick around the corpora cavernosa and thinner around the corpus spongiosum.
The diamond-shaped region below the pelvic diaphragm bounded by the pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments, and coccyx.

sections.title: The broad ligament and the pelvic peritoneal pouches

blocks.text: The uterus rises from the pelvic floor into the peritoneal cavity, and the peritoneum drapes over it like a sheet over a clothesline. Anteriorly the sheet covers the bladder and uterine body; posteriorly it covers the uterus, the posterior fornix of the vagina, and the front of the rectum. Lateral to the uterus the anterior and posterior layers meet as a double fold, the broad ligament, which runs to the lateral pelvic wall and floor. Like a mesentery, it carries vessels, nerves, and lymphatics between its layers.

The broad ligament has three named parts, each named for the organ it suspends. The mesometrium is the largest part, lying beside the uterus and below the other two. The mesosalpinx is the thin upper portion between the uterine tube, which runs in the free upper edge, and the attachment of the ovary. The mesovarium is a short fold projecting from the posterior layer that attaches the ovary. The ovary itself is not covered by peritoneum; its surface epithelium replaces it, so ovulation releases the oocyte directly into the peritoneal cavity near the fimbriae.

blocks.title: Parts and contents of the broad ligament
rows: Largest part, beside the uterus, below the other two
Uterine vessels at its base, round ligament, ovarian ligament, ureter passing beneath at the base
Between the uterine tube and the mesovarium
Uterine tube in its free edge, tubal branches of the uterine and ovarian vessels, mesonephric remnants
Attaches the ovary; carries ovarian vessels into the hilum
blocks.caption: The broad ligament is a mesentery for the uterus, tubes, and ovaries; each part is named for what it suspends (metra, salpinx, ovarium).

blocks.text: Where the peritoneum dips between organs it forms pouches. The vesicouterine pouch between bladder and uterus is shallow. The rectouterine pouch between uterus and rectum is deep, extending down behind the cervix over the posterior vaginal fornix, and it is bounded laterally by the rectouterine folds that contain the uterosacral ligaments. Because it is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in a standing or sitting woman, gravity carries free blood, pus, ascites, and shed tumor cells there. In the male the equivalent lowest recess is the rectovesical pouch. In a supine patient fluid also collects in the hepatorenal recess, the most dependent space of the upper abdomen.

blocks.title: Ruptured tubal pregnancy to the rectouterine pouch
steps: Tubal pregnancy erodes the tubal wall and vessels
Tube ruptures and bleeds into the peritoneal cavity
Blood runs down to the rectouterine pouch
Ultrasound shows fluid behind the uterus
Thin posterior fornix allows needle aspiration (culdocentesis)
blocks.caption: Only the vaginal wall and peritoneum separate the posterior fornix from the pouch, which is why the pouch can be imaged and sampled through the vagina.

blocks.text: The same dependency explains other findings. Blood in the pouch irritates the peritoneum over the rectum, so it can cause a sense of rectal pressure or painful defecation. Pelvic abscesses from salpingitis or a ruptured pelvic appendix collect there and can be felt as a tender, fluctuant mass on vaginal or rectal examination. Endometriosis commonly implants in the pouch and on the uterosacral ligaments, and the resulting scarring can obliterate the pouch and fix the uterus in retroversion.

blocks.predict: A woman with a ruptured ovarian cyst is examined lying flat, then sitting upright. Where does the free fluid collect in each position?
blocks.explain: Lying flat, fluid collects in the most dependent spaces, the pelvic pouch and the hepatorenal recess. Upright, it drains to the rectouterine pouch, the lowest point of the female peritoneal cavity, because the pouch extends down to the posterior vaginal fornix.

sections.title: Named ligaments of the uterus and ovary and the vessels they carry

blocks.text: The named ligaments make sense once you ask where the blood supply comes from. The ovary develops high on the posterior abdominal wall and descends into the pelvis, bringing its vessels with it, so its artery arises from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries and reaches it from above. The uterus develops in the pelvis, so its artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery and reaches it from the side, at the level of the cervix.

The suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament is the lateral upper corner of the broad ligament, running from the ovary and tubal infundibulum to the lateral pelvic wall where it crosses the external iliac vessels. It carries the ovarian vessels, lymphatics, and nerves; ovarian lymph follows them to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes, which matters for ovarian cancer spread. The ureter crosses the pelvic brim just behind this ligament.

Two ligaments are remnants of the female gubernaculum, which attached the gonad to the labioscrotal swelling and became anchored to the side of the uterus near the uterine tube. The part above that attachment is the ovarian ligament (proper ovarian ligament), from the uterine pole of the ovary to the uterus just below the tube; it carries no major vessels. The part below is the round ligament, which leaves the uterus just in front of and below the tube, crosses the pelvic wall, enters the deep inguinal ring, traverses the inguinal canal, and ends in the labium majus, the female counterpart of the scrotum. Stretching of the round ligament in pregnancy causes groin pain.

The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligament is a condensation of fibrous tissue and smooth muscle at the base of the broad ligament, running from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the lateral pelvic wall. The uterine artery and vein run in and just above it toward the cervix. About 2 cm lateral to the cervix the uterine artery passes over the ureter, which runs forward beneath it toward the bladder. The uterosacral ligaments run from the posterior cervix around the rectum to the sacrum within the rectouterine folds; they hold the cervix back, which keeps the uterus anteverted over the bladder.

blocks.caption: Ovarian vessels enter from above in the suspensory ligament; uterine vessels enter from the side at the base of the broad ligament.

blocks.title: Which ligament is involved?
blocks.text: A woman has sudden severe pelvic pain with a large ovarian mass, and Doppler ultrasound shows absent ovarian venous flow. The ovary swings on two attachments: the ovarian ligament medially and the suspensory ligament laterally. Only the suspensory ligament carries the ovarian artery and vein, so twisting of the ovary around these attachments (torsion) kinks the ovarian vessels. The thin-walled veins collapse first, the ovary swells, and arterial inflow then fails, causing ischemia. Because the uterine artery also supplies the ovary through the broad ligament, some arterial flow on Doppler does not exclude torsion.

sections.title: Support of the uterus and vagina and pelvic organ prolapse

blocks.text: Every rise in intra-abdominal pressure from coughing, lifting, or straining pushes the pelvic organs downward, so they need support at several levels. Two systems share the load: an active muscular floor below and passive fibrous suspension above. Prolapse occurs when one system fails and the other is overloaded.

The levator ani forms most of the pelvic diaphragm. Its parts, the puborectalis, pubococcygeus, and iliococcygeus, run from the pubis and the tendinous arch over the obturator internus fascia to the perineal body, anococcygeal ligament, and coccyx. It is supplied by the nerve to levator ani (S3 to S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve. The urethra, vagina, and rectum pass through a gap in front, the urogenital hiatus. Constant resting tone narrows this hiatus and lifts the floor into a firm shelf, so in a standing woman the upper vagina lies almost horizontally on the levator plate and abdominal pressure presses the organs against muscle rather than out through the opening.

The perineal body anchors the lower end of this system. It is a fibromuscular knot between the vagina and anal canal where the bulbospongiosus, superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles, external anal sphincter, and fibers of the levator ani converge. Above, the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments suspend the cervix and upper vagina from the pelvic walls and sacrum, while the middle vagina is attached laterally to the pelvic wall fascia. These fibrous supports work well only while the muscle carries most of the load.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of pelvic organ prolapse
steps: Vaginal delivery stretches or tears levator ani and pudendal nerve
Levator tone falls; urogenital hiatus widens
Vagina becomes more vertical; load shifts to ligaments
Low estrogen, aging, and straining weaken connective tissue
Ligaments stretch; uterus, bladder, or rectum descends
blocks.caption: Muscle failure comes first in most cases; ligaments that are designed for occasional loads then stretch under constant load.

blocks.text: Risk factors follow the mechanism. Vaginal childbirth, especially large infants, prolonged second stage, or forceps delivery, can avulse the pubococcygeus from the pubis and stretch the pudendal nerve. Estrogen loss after menopause reduces collagen content and strength in the pelvic connective tissue and vaginal wall. Obesity, chronic cough, constipation with straining, and heavy lifting raise abdominal pressure, and inherited collagen disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos and Marfan syndromes weaken the fibrous supports from the start.

blocks.title: Types of pelvic relaxation
rows: Cervix and uterus (failed cardinal and uterosacral support)
Down the vaginal canal, to or beyond the introitus
Heavy dragging sensation; exposed cervix may ulcerate from friction and drying
Incomplete emptying and stress incontinence from a hypermobile urethra
Stool trapped in the pouch; incomplete evacuation
Small bowel in the rectouterine pouch
blocks.caption: The organ behind a weakened vaginal wall bulges into the canal; symptoms worsen with standing and straining and ease when lying down.

blocks.text: Grading systems differ between sources, but all describe how far the leading edge descends relative to the hymen or introitus, from descent within the vagina to complete eversion of the uterus outside the body (procidentia). Stress urinary incontinence often accompanies a cystocele because the urethra loses its firm backing of anterior vaginal wall, so a cough no longer compresses it closed.

sections.title: Layers of the scrotum and contents of the spermatic cord

blocks.text: The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and, guided by the gubernaculum, descends through the inguinal canal into the scrotum, usually by birth. A finger of peritoneum, the processus vaginalis, goes ahead of it. As the testis passes through the anterior abdominal wall, each layer of the wall wraps it in a sleeve, so the coverings of the testis and spermatic cord are a map of the abdominal wall.

blocks.title: Coverings collected during testicular descent
steps: Peritoneum: processus vaginalis becomes tunica vaginalis
Deep inguinal ring: transversalis fascia becomes internal spermatic fascia
Internal oblique: cremaster muscle and fascia
Superficial ring: external oblique aponeurosis becomes external spermatic fascia
Scrotum: dartos fascia and skin from superficial fascia and skin
blocks.caption: Read from deep to superficial. The transversus abdominis arches over the cord and contributes no layer.

blocks.title: Scrotal layers from outside in
rows: Thin, pigmented, without fat; lymph to superficial inguinal nodes
Superficial fascia, continuous with Colles and Scarpa fascia
Smooth muscle wrinkles the skin in cold, reducing heat loss
Skeletal muscle that raises the testis; supplied by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Serous sac around the front and sides of the testis; fluid here is a hydrocele
blocks.caption: The cord has the three spermatic coverings; the tunica vaginalis surrounds only the testis. The tunica albuginea of the testis lies deep to its visceral layer.

blocks.text: The spermatic cord runs from the deep inguinal ring to the posterior border of the testis. Its contents are the ductus deferens, which feels like a firm cord at the back of the bundle; the testicular artery from the abdominal aorta; the artery to the ductus from a vesical artery; the cremasteric artery from the inferior epigastric artery; the pampiniform venous plexus; the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve; sympathetic and visceral afferent fibers on the arteries; lymphatics that drain the testis to para-aortic nodes; and any remnant of the processus vaginalis. The ilioinguinal nerve runs on the cord, outside its coverings.

Spermatogenesis works best a few degrees below core temperature, about 2 to 3 °C (3.6 to 5.4 °F) lower. The pampiniform plexus surrounds the testicular artery so that cooler venous blood draws heat from arterial blood before it reaches the testis, a countercurrent exchange. The dartos and cremaster tighten the scrotum and raise the testis in cold. The cremasteric reflex (stroking the medial thigh raises the testis) uses the L1 to L2 segments through the genitofemoral and ilioinguinal nerves, and it is usually absent in testicular torsion.

The plexus converges into the testicular vein near the deep ring. The left vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle and the right enters the inferior vena cava obliquely, so dilation of the plexus (varicocele) is far more common on the left. A varicocele feels like a bag of worms, fills on standing, and impairs cooling. A new right-sided varicocele, or one that does not empty when the patient lies down, suggests obstruction of venous outflow by a retroperitoneal mass. A processus vaginalis that stays open allows peritoneal fluid into the tunica vaginalis (communicating hydrocele) or bowel into the cord coverings (indirect inguinal hernia).

blocks.predict: A 3-cm testicular tumor spreads by lymphatics. Which nodes enlarge first, and would the answer change for a carcinoma of the scrotal skin?
blocks.explain: Testicular lymph follows the testicular vessels back to their origin, so it drains to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near the renal vessels. Scrotal skin drains like the rest of the lower abdominal and perineal skin, to superficial inguinal nodes.

sections.title: Position of the breast and the suspensory ligaments

blocks.text: The breast is a modified sweat gland that lies within the superficial fascia of the anterior chest wall. Its base extends vertically from about the second to the sixth rib and transversely from the lateral border of the sternum to about the midaxillary line. About two thirds of the base rests on the pectoral fascia over the pectoralis major and the rest on the fascia over the serratus anterior. A small extension, the axillary tail, passes along the lower edge of the pectoralis major toward the axilla, so breast tissue and its tumors can appear as an axillary mass.

Between the breast and the pectoral fascia lies the retromammary space, a layer of loose connective tissue that lets the normal breast glide over the chest wall. The gland consists of about 15 to 20 lobes, each drained by a lactiferous duct that opens on the nipple. Fibrous septa between the lobes condense into the suspensory ligaments (Cooper ligaments), which run from the dermis of the skin through the breast to the deep fascia. They support the breast, and their gradual stretching with age, pregnancy, and weight change allows the breast to sag.

These attachments explain the classic signs of carcinoma. Invasive carcinoma provokes a desmoplastic reaction, a dense fibrous stroma that contracts as it matures. When the tumor infiltrates suspensory ligaments, their shortening pulls the overlying skin inward, causing dimpling (skin retraction) that becomes obvious when the patient raises her arms or presses her hands on her hips. Involvement of the lactiferous ducts behind the nipple shortens them and causes nipple retraction. Tumor that invades through the retromammary space into the pectoral fascia fixes the mass, so it no longer moves when the pectoralis major contracts.

blocks.title: Breast signs and the structure responsible
rows: Tumor and desmoplastic fibrosis shorten the ligaments and pull the skin inward
Fibrosis shortens the ducts behind the nipple
Tumor emboli block lymph flow; edematous skin is tethered at hair follicles and pores
Breast tissue extends toward the axilla, and most breast lymph drains to axillary nodes
blocks.caption: Each sign localizes the tumor to a particular part of the breast framework; acquired nipple retraction differs from a lifelong inverted nipple.

blocks.text: Most lymph from the breast, about three quarters, drains to the axillary nodes, and most of the rest drains to parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels, so medial tumors may spread inside the chest. The upper outer quadrant contains the most glandular tissue, which is why most carcinomas arise there. Accessory nipples or breast tissue can appear anywhere along the embryonic mammary ridge from the axilla to the groin.

blocks.predict: Two women have a firm breast mass. In one the skin over it dimples when she raises her arms; in the other the skin is thick and pitted over a red, warm breast. Which structure is involved in each?
blocks.explain: Dimpling means the tumor has shortened the suspensory ligaments that tether the skin. Thick pitted skin (peau d'orange) means tumor emboli are blocking dermal lymphatics, so the skin is edematous except where hair follicles tether it, as in inflammatory carcinoma.

sections.title: Erectile bodies of the penis and penile fracture

blocks.text: The penis has a fixed root in the urogenital triangle of the perineum and a free body. The root contains three erectile masses: two crura, attached to the ischiopubic rami and covered by the ischiocavernosus muscles, and the midline bulb, attached to the perineal membrane and covered by the bulbospongiosus. In the body, the crura continue as the paired corpora cavernosa on the dorsal side, and the bulb continues as the single corpus spongiosum on the ventral side. The corpus spongiosum surrounds the spongy urethra and expands distally into the glans.

Each erectile body is wrapped in a tunica albuginea of dense collagen with some elastic fibers. Around the corpora cavernosa it is thick and forms a midline septum that is incomplete, so the two corpora fill as one unit. Around the corpus spongiosum it is thinner and more elastic. All three bodies are then enclosed by the deep fascia of the penis (Buck fascia), and outside that lie the loose superficial (dartos) fascia and thin skin.

blocks.title: How the tunica albuginea produces rigidity
steps: Pelvic splanchnic (S2 to S4) fibers release nitric oxide
cGMP rises; arterial and trabecular smooth muscle relaxes
Blood fills the cavernous sinusoids
Expanding sinusoids compress venules against the tunica
Venous outflow falls; pressure rises toward arterial levels
blocks.caption: Veno-occlusion depends on an intact, inextensible tunica albuginea around the corpora cavernosa.

blocks.text: The thick tunica around the corpora cavernosa is what lets intracavernous pressure rise high enough for rigidity, because a stretchy wall would simply expand. The thinner tunica around the corpus spongiosum keeps that body at lower pressure during erection, so the urethra stays open for ejaculation and the glans stays relatively soft.

Erection stretches the tunica and makes it much thinner and stiffer, so a sudden bending force on the erect penis, usually during intercourse, can tear it. This is penile fracture: a rupture of the tunica albuginea of one or both corpora cavernosa. The patient typically reports a cracking sound, sharp pain, and immediate loss of erection as the pressurized blood escapes. Blood collects under the skin, and the shaft swells, discolors, and often deviates away from the side of the tear.

The distribution of the hematoma depends on the fascia. While Buck fascia is intact, blood is confined to the shaft. If Buck fascia also tears, blood spreads in the plane beneath the membranous superficial fascia into the scrotum, perineum, and lower abdominal wall. Because the corpus spongiosum lies against the corpora cavernosa, a minority of fractures also injure the urethra, signaled by blood at the meatus, hematuria, or inability to void. A localized, painless plaque of fibrosis in the tunica albuginea (Peyronie disease) causes curvature of the erect penis by the same principle in reverse: the scarred side cannot lengthen.

blocks.title: Tracing a hematoma by fascial planes
blocks.text: A man has a perineal straddle injury, followed by swelling and bruising of the scrotum, penis, and lower abdominal wall, but not the thighs. Ask which plane the blood is in. The membranous superficial fascia of the perineum (Colles fascia) attaches posteriorly to the perineal membrane and laterally to the ischiopubic rami, then continues into the scrotum as dartos and onto the abdomen as the membranous layer (Scarpa fascia), which fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament. Blood or urine from a ruptured bulbar urethra fills this space, so it cannot pass into the thighs or the anal triangle. A penile fracture with intact Buck fascia stays on the shaft instead.

sections.title: Boundaries of the perineum and the position of the prostate

blocks.text: The perineum is the region below the pelvic diaphragm (levator ani and coccygeus) and between the thighs. Its outline is the inferior pelvic outlet, a diamond whose corners and sides are bony and ligamentous landmarks that can be felt or pictured on a skeleton. A transverse line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into two triangles that lie in different planes, the urogenital triangle facing downward and forward and the anal triangle facing downward and backward.

blocks.title: Boundaries and divisions of the perineum
rows: Attachment of the perineal membrane, crura, and Colles fascia
A line between them separates the two triangles
Covered by the lower border of gluteus maximus
Perineal membrane, superficial and deep perineal pouches, external genitalia, urethra, and vagina in the female
Anal canal, external anal sphincter, fat-filled ischioanal fossae, pudendal canal on their lateral walls
blocks.caption: The perineal body lies at the center of the diamond, where the two triangles meet.

blocks.text: The structures in each triangle explain several clinical patterns. The pudendal nerve (S2 to S4), which supplies perineal skin, the external anal and urethral sphincters, and the perineal muscles, runs in the pudendal canal in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa, so it can be anesthetized near the ischial spine. The ischioanal fossae communicate behind the anal canal, which allows an abscess on one side to spread around to the other.

The prostate is a fibromuscular gland that surrounds the first part of the male urethra. Its base lies against the neck of the bladder, its apex rests on the external urethral sphincter in the deep perineal pouch, and its posterior surface faces the rectum, separated from it only by the thin rectoprostatic fascia (Denonvilliers fascia). Because the anterior rectal wall is thin, a finger in the rectum feels the posterior surface: two lateral lobes separated by a shallow median sulcus. A normal gland feels smooth and rubbery, about the size of a walnut. The seminal vesicles lie above it, behind the bladder, and are normally out of reach.

blocks.title: Prostate zones and what the rectal examination detects
rows: Posterior and lateral, against the rectum; most of the glandular tissue
Hard, irregular nodule; median sulcus may be lost
Smooth, symmetric, rubbery enlargement; may feel nearly normal while still compressing the urethra
Around the ejaculatory ducts at the base
blocks.caption: Rectal examination samples the posterior gland, which favors detection of peripheral zone cancer over transition zone hyperplasia.

blocks.text: This explains why benign hyperplasia and carcinoma behave differently. Hyperplastic nodules grow in the transition zone around the urethra, so they cause obstructive urinary symptoms early, even when the palpable surface feels only moderately enlarged. Carcinoma arises mainly in the peripheral zone, far from the urethra, so it often causes no urinary symptoms until it is advanced, but it is the zone the examining finger reaches first.

integration.text: Embryology and anatomy explain most of this chapter. The gubernaculum and processus vaginalis account for the inguinal course of both the round ligament and the spermatic cord, the abdominal wall origin of each scrotal layer, and the hernias and hydroceles that follow a patent processus. Gonads keep their abdominal blood supply and lymph drainage after descent, so ovarian and testicular cancers spread first to para-aortic nodes while the skin of the scrotum and vulva drains to inguinal nodes. The peritoneum explains the broad ligament and its pouches, and fascial continuities, such as Colles fascia with the dartos and Scarpa fascia, predict how blood and urine spread.

Physiology and pathology act on this framework. Gravity sends blood, pus, and tumor cells to the rectouterine pouch; collagen loss with low estrogen and muscle injury from childbirth explain prolapse; desmoplastic fibrosis in breast carcinoma turns the suspensory ligaments into a visible sign; the inextensible tunica albuginea is both the basis of rigidity and the structure that fractures; and the zonal anatomy of the prostate decides whether disease obstructs the urethra or is felt on rectal examination. These findings localize disease but do not establish its nature, which requires imaging or tissue diagnosis.

summary: The broad ligament is a double peritoneal fold divided into mesometrium (uterus), mesosalpinx (tube), and mesovarium (ovary).
The rectouterine pouch is the lowest point of the female peritoneal cavity when upright; blood or pus collects there and is reached through the posterior vaginal fornix.

Ovarian vessels run in the suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament from above; uterine vessels run at the base of the broad ligament with the cardinal ligament and cross over the ureter near the cervix.
The ovarian ligament and the round ligament are remnants of the gubernaculum; the round ligament traverses the inguinal canal to the labium majus.
Levator ani tone keeps the urogenital hiatus closed; when it fails, the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments stretch and the uterus, bladder, or rectum prolapses into the vagina.

Scrotal layers mirror the abdominal wall: external oblique to external spermatic fascia, internal oblique to cremaster, transversalis fascia to internal spermatic fascia, peritoneum to tunica vaginalis.

The spermatic cord carries the ductus deferens, testicular artery, pampiniform plexus, and genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve; the plexus cools arterial blood, and left varicoceles predominate because of left testicular vein drainage.
The breast lies on pectoralis major and serratus anterior from about rib 2 to rib 6 with an axillary tail; carcinoma that shortens the suspensory ligaments dimples the skin.
Two dorsal corpora cavernosa and a ventral corpus spongiosum around the urethra are wrapped in tunica albuginea; tearing it in the erect penis is a penile fracture.
The perineum is a diamond divided into urogenital and anal triangles; the prostate lies below the bladder and in front of the rectum, so its peripheral zone is felt on rectal examination.

verify: The cardinal ligament is described in some texts as carrying the uterine vessels and in others as lying just below them at the base of the broad ligament; this chapter states that the vessels run in and just above it.
The distance at which the uterine artery crosses the ureter is quoted as about 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix; confirm the figure NABNE expects.
Testicular temperature below core is quoted from about 2 to 4 °C (3.6 to 7.2 °F) in different sources; this chapter uses about 2 to 3 °C.
The vertical extent of the breast is given as rib 2 to rib 6 by Moore; some sources give the 2nd to 6th intercostal level or rib 2 to rib 7.
The share of breast lymph draining to axillary nodes is commonly given as about 75%, but values vary by source and method.
The proportion of prostate carcinomas arising in the peripheral zone is quoted from about 70% to 80%; this chapter says most.
The proportion of penile fractures with urethral injury varies widely between series; this chapter says a minority.
Pelvic organ prolapse grading (degree systems and the POP-Q system) differs between sources; confirm whether NABNE Part I tests a specific scheme.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms pouch of Douglas, Cooper ligaments, Buck fascia, Colles fascia, Scarpa fascia, and Denonvilliers fascia, or only descriptive names.
